answers.query: Why does AI make things up?

request.query: Why does AI make things up?

payload.answer: Here is what I found in LAiDIES. These references may answer part of your question.

results.title: "How often does AI make stuff up?"
results.summary: Confidence: It depends It makes things up — but less, and less randomly, than the panic suggests. How often depends entirely on what you ask: hand it a document to summarize and the top models are very reliable; ask it to recall a fact from memory and it's much shakier. What's solid — There is no honest single hallucination rate.…

results.title: 11.6 — Hallucination: Why It Makes Things Up
results.summary: You've probably experienced this: you ask an AI to recommend a book, and it gives you a title, an author, a publication year, even a one-paragraph summary. It sounds perfect. You search for it and the book doesn't exist. The author is real. The topic is real. The title is plausible. But the book was never written. The model didn't lie to you — it has no concept of lying.…

results.title: 1.2 — What Isn't AI (And Why It Still Matters)
results.summary: Now that you've seen the seam in one place, let's make sure it holds up everywhere. Here are things you use every day that are impressive, useful, sometimes even remarkable — but are not AI. Your calculator. You type 7 × 8. It says 56. It will always say 56. A human being wrote the multiplication rules into it decades ago, and it follows those rules every single time, perfectly, without deviation.…

results.title: Structural constraint
results.summary: A rule that gives the AI something concrete to DO (or not do) rather than a vague prohibition. "Use only information from this document" works. "Don't make things up" doesn't. Read the full explanation .

results.title: What Wastes Your Context Budget (Despite Being Widely Taught)
results.summary: Some techniques that appear in older guides now make things worse on 2026 models. If you've been taught these, it's not your fault. The models changed; the advice on the internet didn't. "Never hallucinate" and similar prohibitions. Telling the AI what NOT to do ("don't make things up," "never invent facts") doesn't create a constraint it can enforce.…

results.title: Context compaction
results.summary: What happens when the AI's working memory fills up: the tool silently compresses older messages into a shorter summary to make room. Details get lost without warning. You'll notice it as the AI "forgetting" things you told it earlier. Read the full explanation .

results.title: 1.4 — When a Product Uses Both (Most of Them Do)
results.summary: In real life, you don't encounter "AI" and "not AI" as separate things. You encounter products — and most products have both going on at the same time, in the same app, working together. One product can contain both: a fixed rule routes known conditions; a learned model handles pattern-based decisions. Gmail. You wrote a filter: "anything from noreply@store.com goes to my Promotions tab." That fires every time, exactly as you set it up.…

results.title: 10.5 Setting Up One Recurring Task
results.summary: Start with one. Pick the most boring, repeatable thinking task you do every week. Something where: The input is predictable (same sources each time) The output format is consistent (same structure each time) The quality bar is clear (you'd know immediately if it's wrong) Doing it manually is tedious but not deeply creative Examples: Weekly report compilation from multiple sources Meeting prep notes based on calendar + recent context Sta…

results.title: 13.3 Staying Current (Without Making It a Second Job)
results.summary: AI tools change every few months. New models, new features, new modes, new names for old things. It's like trying to follow every cast change on a soap opera. You'll exhaust yourself and miss the plot anyway. Don't try to keep up with everything. What actually works: Pick ONE primary tool and learn it deeply. You'll get more from mastering one platform than superficially knowing five. Depth beats breadth for daily productivity.…

results.title: Context window
results.summary: The maximum number of tokens a system can "see" at once — its working memory for a single conversation Read the full explanation . Put it into practice .

results.title: Context
results.summary: Everything the model can "see" right now — your message, the conversation history, system instructions, retrieved documents. All in one window. Read the full explanation . Put it into practice .

results.title: OpenAI is expanding ChatGPT ads. Here’s what’s paid for.
results.summary:
Suppose you ask ChatGPT for somewhere to take six colleagues for lunch. You mention the neighbourhood and budget. Those details give the system context: information about what you need. OpenAI says its advertising system can use the current conversation to choose a relevant ad, separately from the system generating the answer.

A restaurant could therefore pay to appear beside that lunch discussion. That does not mean it won the comparison in the answer. OpenAI says advertisers cannot alter the response, and that ads are labelled and separate. Those are the company’s stated rules, not an independent audit.

results.title: 15.3 — Context Engineering (mid-2025): Everything It Can See
results.summary: What it is: Designing the complete context window — not just the prompt, but everything the model can access when it generates a response. The shift: People realised that the quality of AI output depends less on how you phrase the question and more on what information the model has access to when answering. The prompt matters, but it's maybe 10% of what determines output quality. The other 90% is: what documents were retrieved?…

results.title: 📖 Key Terms — Quick Reference
results.summary: Context window Everything the model can see for this specific request. Conversation history + system instructions + retrieved documents + your message. Hard size limit (1M+ tokens for frontier models, 2026). Stateless The model itself remembers nothing between requests. Each inference is independent. "Memory" is external systems re-injecting information. Embedding A list of numbers (vector) that represents the meaning of text.…

results.title: 10.4 — System Prompts: The Hidden Instructions
results.summary: Before your message ever reaches the model, the system loads system instructions — a hidden prompt that goes into the context window first. You never see this, but it shapes everything about how the model responds. A system prompt might say: "You are a helpful assistant. Be concise. Use British English." "You are a customer support agent for [Company]. Only answer questions about our products.…

Diffusion: start from pure noise, remove noise step by step, guided by your text description via cross-attention. Not "creating from nothing" — sculpting randomness into structure How does image editing work?…

results.summary: Test the "no memory" principle. Open a new conversation with any AI chatbot. Ask it: "What's my name?" It won't know — because nothing in the context window tells it. Now tell it your name, have a short conversation, then start a new conversation and ask again. Gone. The first conversation's context isn't in the new window. Test semantic search thinking.…

payload.answer: Here is what I found in LAiDIES. These references may answer part of your question.

results.title: 15.2 — Prompt Engineering (2023): How You Ask
results.summary: What it is: The craft of phrasing your instruction to the model in a way that produces good output. What practitioners do: Write clear, specific instructions Structure prompts with examples (few-shot) Test different phrasings to find what works Add constraints ("respond in JSON," "maximum 3 sentences") Use techniques like chain-of-thought ("think step by step") The scope: One message. One call.…

results.title: The Standard Handover Prompt
results.summary: "Before we end, write a complete handover I can paste into a new conversation. Include: our goal, current status, key decisions we've made, what to avoid, and the very next step. Be specific (use exact names, numbers, and details) rather than vague summaries. Structure it so a new session can continue immediately without needing this conversation's full history."

results.title: 15.1 — The Same Job Got Renamed Four Times
results.summary: In 2023, someone got hired as a "prompt engineer." Their job: write really good instructions for AI systems. They got good at it. They learned all the tricks — chain-of-thought, few-shot examples, structured formatting. By 2025, their LinkedIn title changed to "context engineer" — same person, same desk, same company.…

results.title: AI predicts later cancer spread. Better care is the next test.
results.summary:
Think of a weather forecast warning that rain is coming. Getting the forecast right does not tell you whether a particular roof repair will keep your room dry. You need evidence about the repair too. In health AI, those are likewise two different questions: can we identify a risk, and does acting on that information help?

Some records came from a registered treatment trial. That trial compared chemotherapy approaches; it did not assign care using this AI. The new paper looked back at a selected group from it. A trial in the source material is not automatically a trial of the new tool.

Most records came from Chinese hospitals, and performance varied by treatment group. The authors call for wider international testing and report practical implementation challenges. Funding includes public programmes and a Hengrui pharmaceutical research partnership; the authors declare no competing interests. We have not verified an independent replication.

There is an independent yardstick for the next step. The International Medical Device Regulators Forum’s guiding principles call for testing that represents the intended patients—including sex and gender—and evaluates how peop

results.title: The FAiRY Godmother
results.summary: The town's real AI assistant — bring a question or a rough prompt and she gives advice and glows it up.

results.title: "Is AI's energy use getting better or worse?"
results.summary: Confidence: Contested Both at once — and that's a race, not a verdict. Every query keeps getting more efficient, while total energy use keeps climbing because we keep using so much more of it. What's solid — Efficiency per task is improving, but total demand is growing faster.…

results.title: 15.7 — What These People Actually Do (Day-to-Day)
results.summary: Stripped of hype, what work at each level looks like: Prompt engineering (still the most common): Writing and iterating on system prompts Testing prompt variations and measuring which produces better results Documenting "prompt patterns" that reliably work for specific tasks Teaching non-technical colleagues how to get better results from AI tools Context engineering: Building and maintaining RAG pipelines Deciding how to chunk document…

results.title: 4.3 The Brief (Not the Prompt)
results.summary: The word "prompt" implies a single clever sentence that unlocks the AI's potential. The reality in 2026 is closer to writing a brief: a short, structured description that gives a smart but uninformed executor everything they need to produce what you want. An agent can sometimes pause or ask for clarification, but you should not depend on that happening at the right moment.…

results.title: 5.9 — Scaling Laws: Why Bigger Kept Being Better
results.summary: In 2020, researchers at OpenAI published a striking finding: if you make a language model bigger (more parameters), train it on more data, and give it more compute — its performance improves in a smooth, predictable way. Not in jumps. Not randomly. Along a clean curve. These scaling laws became the roadmap for the entire industry.…

results.title: Tell Me What You Want
results.summary: Episode 2 — prompting is delegation: give context, be specific, hand over an example.

results.title: 6.2 The Three-Attempt Rule
results.summary: Academic research on AI repair loops (2026) found a consistent pattern: "the first three to four repair iterations account for most achievable gains, while later iterations contribute only marginal improvements." Practitioners confirm this independently. Multiple sources report the same observation: fresh sessions outperform heavily corrected ones more often than most people expect.…
